recordings.text: Look at that: one piece attacking several targets at the same moment. A fork, and a very busy piece.
Curious how much one enemy piece could do from here. A fork is now possible for the other side, with several targets under attack at once.
Another move contained a fork, one piece hitting several targets together. This move goes a different way and leaves it unused.
Interesting. This piece looks free, yet it is pinned to its king. It may slide along the line, but stepping off it would expose the king.
Now a pin to the king becomes possible for the other side. A piece caught that way can only move along the line; stepping off it would expose its own king.
A different move would have fixed an enemy piece to its king, since leaving the line would have exposed the king. A pin, unplayed.
A skewer. The attack lands on the front piece, and when it steps away, the piece behind it on the same line is exposed. Two targets, arranged in a queue.
This permits a skewer: an attack on a front piece that, once it moves, exposes whatever stands behind it.
A skewer was available in a stronger move: attack the front piece, and once it moves aside, the one behind it is exposed.
The point is to capture a defender. Watch what that defender was protecting; that is what loses its cover.
Now the other side can capture a defender, and whatever it protected may be left without cover.
Another move could have captured a defender, stripping the protection from whatever it guarded.
Fascinating, really: the king is shut in by its own pieces. That is the back-rank mate idea.
This opens a route to a back-rank mate for the other side. The king's own pieces are the ones blocking its escape.
There was a back-rank mate available, the enemy king trapped behind its own pieces. This move does not take it.
This is about promotion. Should the pawn reach the last rank, it changes into a new piece. Such a small piece, with such a large future.
This gives the other side a chance to promote. One of their pawns could reach the last rank and turn into a new piece.
A stronger move offered a route to promotion. This move leaves that pawn short of the last rank.
A discovered attack. The moving piece clears the way; the real attack comes from the piece that was hidden behind it, along the newly opened line.
A discovered attack is now possible: one piece moves aside, and a threat appears from the piece behind it.
A discovered attack was sitting in another move: one piece steps aside, and a threat appears from the piece behind.
Two threats launched by one move: a double attack. The defense now has two problems to solve at once.
A double attack becomes available to the other side: one move, two threats.
A stronger move contained a double attack, two threats in one move. This move does not find it.
A deflection. The defender is drawn away from its duty, and what it was guarding is left exposed.
This gives the other side a chance at a deflection, pulling a defender away from its task, so whatever it guarded is left open.
Another move could have pulled a defender away from its duty. That deflection would have left what it guarded uncovered.
Before anything clever, check for pieces with no defender. Here there is one, and the idea is simply to take it.
With a different move, an undefended piece was there for the taking. This one passes over it, and nothing was guarding it at all.
After this move, one piece has no defender, and the other side can take it.
A convincing move on its own, but it removes a piece's only real defender. Now the other side can capture the piece that was left behind.
The opponent's previous move carried a threat, and this one does not respond to it. One of the pieces is now open to capture.
This capture is answered by a recapture of something more valuable. An exchange is only finished when both captures are counted.
A minor piece leaves its starting square and enters the game. Development, plainly visible.
With a different move, a minor piece would have come off its starting square into play.
An open file, and the rook is on it. From one end to the other, no pawn of either color.
With a different move, a rook could have occupied an open file, one without a single pawn on it.
A semi-open file, and the rook is on it: no friendly pawn there, though an enemy pawn is still somewhere along it.
A different move would have placed a rook on a semi-open file: no friendly pawn on it, but at least one enemy pawn.
A passed pawn. Look along its file and both neighboring files: no enemy pawn stands ahead.
Another move would have created a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or the neighboring files.
The pawn was already passed, and this move pushes it further forward. Each step brings it nearer the last rank.
With a different move, the passed pawn could have advanced another step.
An isolated pawn is the result. No friendly pawn stands on either neighboring file.
A different move would have left an isolated pawn, lacking any friendly pawn on the neighboring files.
Before this move, a piece stood undefended. Now a defender covers it. A new connection on the board.
A different move would have found a defender for a piece that had none.
After this move, a piece has no defender. Undefended describes the piece; it does not prove the piece can be won.
A different move would have left a piece undefended; that alone would not have made it winnable.
This move opens a fresh legal square for the king. A small exit, newly made.
With a different move, the king would have gained a new flight square.
The king castles, and the rook settles on the king's other side. Two pieces relocated in one move.
Castling was the alternative: king and rook relocated in one move.
With this capture, a bishop pair is broken. The side that lost the bishop now covers only one square color with bishops.
With a different move, a bishop would have been captured and the other side's bishop pair broken.
Doubled pawns: one file now holds two pawns of the same color.
With a different move, two pawns of one color would have ended up on a single file: doubled pawns.
With this move, a forced checkmate opens up for the other side. The path of that attack is worth tracing, move by move.
The finish was there: a forced checkmate with another move. This one goes past it. That mate is worth finding now.
The material looks lost, and yet the sacrifice holds. In the searched line, accepting it does not refute the idea.
A very narrow margin. Among all the searched moves, this was the single one that kept the position playable; every alternative was losing.
The advantage survived through this move alone. Among the searched moves, every other choice was losing.
The reply comes at once: the other side can capture something immediately.
The strongest reply is a check, so the king comes first; everything else waits.
The engine prefers another move here. Play it on the board and compare what the replies do.
By the engine's measure, this move is weaker than the best option. The reply shows where the difference appears.
Strong. Among the moves the engine examined, this one stands up well.
A solid decision. It keeps much of what the position offered, even if the engine has another first choice.
This move appears in the opening catalogue, part of a documented line.
Here the game steps off the documented opening line for the first time. From this move on, it is its own.
After the earlier setback, the position is playable again with this move. An earlier error, not a final one.
This brings back a playable position after the earlier setback, and errors from the other side helped make it possible.
The opponent's previous move offered a chance, and this move uses it. One side's lapse, the other side's opportunity.
The opponent's last move offered an opportunity, and this move passes over it. A stronger answer was available.
This same issue appeared earlier in the game too. When something repeats, I start paying closer attention. Compare the moments where it appeared.
Earlier, this piece was left unguarded. Now it has a defender again.
No single move did the damage here. This is one of several small concessions that, together, have worsened the position.
The advantage was kept through the reviewed moves, right through to the recorded win. That stretch shows how an edge is held.
This issue also shows up in other saved games. Collected together, those examples say more than any one of them alone.
Checkmate. Not one legal escape remains for the king. Every exit closed, and the attack complete.
Checkmate. Your king has no legal move out of check. The decisions worth examining come earlier, before the attack arrived.
A draw ends the game. A settled result, though the decisions along the way are still worth examining.
I'll watch with interest. Study the position, then choose your move.
That attempt does not stand up. Re-examine the board and attempt a different move.
That attempt produced no result. Return to the move and try once more.
The saved engine analysis shows a forced checkmate for the side that played this move.
The saved engine analysis shows the other side with a forced checkmate after this move.
Tally the material across the saved line: the side that played this move finishes above where it began.
Tally the material across the saved line: the side that played this move finishes below where it began.
This move is accepted for the exercise, though the moves shown give no clear tactical explanation. Accepted, and still a small mystery.
This move is not accepted for the exercise, and the moves shown do not reveal a clear tactical reason why.
This move matches one of the saved answers, and for this exercise the saved answers are what decide acceptance.
This move falls outside the saved answers for the exercise. Outside the answers is not the same as bad chess.
Examine the move closely, then go on to the next position.
Good move. Remember why it works, not only what it was.
Practice saved. Nothing about your review schedule has changed.
Solved. This recall remains marked for relearning.
This is the starting position, before any of the moves under examination.
Movement detected. Observe what has changed.
This move gives check, so the king's safety must be answered first.
With this move, the king escapes the check.
Last rank reached; the pawn promotes. A pawn no longer.
The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes, giving check at the same time.
The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes, and it is checkmate. No legal square is left for the king.
Promotion on the last rank, and with the same move, its king is no longer in check.
A capture: one piece is removed from the board.
A capture that also gives check. Two things accomplished by one move.
Capture and checkmate in one move. The king has no legal answer.
This capture removes the check on its own king as well.
A pawn capture on the last rank, and promotion on the same square.
One pawn move does three things: it captures on the last rank, promotes, and gives check.
The pawn captures on the last rank, promotes, and with that, checkmate: every legal escape for the king is gone.
A capture on the last rank, a promotion, and the end of the check against its own king, all from one pawn move.
The king castles, the rook jumps to its new square, and the move gives check as well.
The king castles, the rook takes its new square, and it is checkmate, with no legal escape for the opposing king. A rare way to finish, and a memorable one.
Follow the forking piece: it attacks several targets at once, then collects one. In this example the material count also ends in that side's favor, by a net gain.
The piece cannot make the indicated capture, because it is pinned to its king. Stepping off the pin line would expose the king.
The attacked piece is pinned to its king, so it cannot simply run. Only moves that keep the king shielded are allowed.
The defenders are pinned to their king, so they cannot recapture there; that is why the capture works. The line shown includes a material gain.
Observe the pinned piece. It cannot leave its line without exposing its king, and as these moves unfold, it is captured.
Once the front piece steps aside, the attacker reaches through and captures the piece that was behind it.
Here the king is in check along the line and has to step away. Once it does, the same attacker collects the piece that stood behind it.
Two captures in sequence: the only defender first, then the piece it guarded. Without the first, the second would not be possible.
The defender is drawn away from its duty, and the piece it was guarding is then captured.
The blocker steps aside, the piece behind it gains a line, and it makes the capture along that line.
The moving piece clears the way, and check comes from a different piece behind it.
Double check: two pieces attack the king at the same instant. Remarkable, the efficiency of it.
The first piece makes its own attack and opens a line for another. In this example, that second piece captures its target.
Follow the pawn until it promotes. In this example, that side also finishes with a net material gain.
The undefended piece is captured, and in this example the capturing side comes away with a net material gain.
A relative pin on the attacking piece was lifted by the opponent's previous move. The next move left the target standing where it was, and the shown line captures it.
The other side has a legal reply, marked on the board. Make it there and observe what follows.
Before moving, check which of your pieces could be captured with no useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, look for enemy pieces that are not defended.
Examine forcing moves in which one piece attacks two valuable targets together.
Behind every pinned piece is something it protects: perhaps the king, perhaps a piece worth more. Inspect that before moving it.
Look beyond the first target. An attack along the line can expose a more valuable piece behind it.
Before exchanging a defender, find out what it is protecting at the moment.
Notice which lines open when a blocking piece moves away.
Search for a single move that makes two threats, counting checks and newly opened lines.
Before moving a back-rank defender, look at the king's escape squares.
Count how far the pawn is from promotion, and examine the forcing pawn advances.
Before moving a defender, see which pieces would lose its protection.
An exchange has two parts: what you capture, and what their recapture takes back. Count both before judging.
Check whether a forcing exchange could pull a defender away from another target.
For this exercise, the saved answers set the rule. Another legal move is not necessarily bad chess.
The moves shown answer each turn with a strong reply; none of those replies is necessarily forced.
These material changes belong to the shown line only, counted from where it began. For the piece values used, see the written explanation.
The saved line holds no simple tactical reason. Play through it and set the replies against each other; nothing positional has been inferred.
The exercise has a saved answer policy, and this explanation follows it. You can see the setting in the written notes.

The full solution, with no wrong moves. Fascinating to watch it found so cleanly.
